Mockolate is a modern, strongly-typed, AOT-compatible mocking library for .NET, powered by source generators. It enables fast, compile-time validated mocking with .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 8, .NET 10, .NET 11 and .NET Framework 4.8. IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); bool success = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 4); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); When the dispenser was not called, the verification throws a MockVerificationException: Failure message Expected that mock invoked method Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) exactly once, but it never did.

Source generator-based: No runtime proxy generation. Fast: Direct dispatch with no reflection or dynamic proxies. Strongly-typed: Compile-time safety and IntelliSense support. AOT compatible: Works with Native AOT and trimming. Modern C#: First-class support for ref structs, static interface members, and current language features. Reflection-based mocks (Moq, NSubstitute, …) Mockolate AOT / trimming not supported supported Validation runtime exceptions analyzers + compile errors Setup API Expression<Func<…>> trees regular method calls Hot path dynamic-proxy dispatch direct dispatch See the side-by-side comparison with Moq, NSubstitute and FakeItEasy, and the benchmarks for performance numbers.

The basics of creating, setting up and verifying mocks cover most tests. The following features help in the remaining cases: Feature Use it when you want to … Protected members set up or verify protected virtual members of a class mock Static interface members mock static abstract or static virtual interface members Advanced callback features control how often and when return values and callbacks apply Monitor interactions only verify the interactions within a scope, or reset the recorded interactions Check for unexpected interactions make sure every interaction was verified, or every setup was used Scenarios switch between sets of setups, for collaborators with an internal state For example, scenarios let a dispenser with a Refill method behave differently before and after a refill: public interface IChocolateDispenser { // the members from the core concepts, and: bool Refill(int amount); } dispenser.Mock.InScenario("empty").Setup.Refill(It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .TransitionTo("loaded"); dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded").Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true);

Returns, Throws and Do entries form a sequence: each call uses the next entry, and after the last entry the sequence starts over. The following modifiers change how an entry takes part in the sequence. They work on methods, properties, indexers and events alike. Modifier Effect .When(predicate) applies the entry only when the predicate on the invocation counter is true .For(n) uses the entry for n calls in a row before moving on .Only(n) uses the entry at most n times in total; .OnlyOnce() is short for .Only(1) .Forever() uses the entry for all further calls; the sequence no longer starts over .InParallel() runs a Do callback on every call, alongside the sequence

Execute a callback or return a value only when the zero-based invocation counter satisfies a predicate: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Called!")).When(count => count >= 2); // The first two calls are skipped

Use an entry for several calls in a row before moving on to the next one: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("First three calls")).For(3) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Next three calls")).For(3); dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .Returns(10).For(1) .Returns(20).For(2) .Returns(30).For(3); // Reads: 10, 20, 20, 30, 30, 30, 10, 20, 20, …

Stop using an entry after it was used a number of times: // Execute the callback up to 3 times dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Up to 3 times")).Only(3); // Throw only on the first read dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .Throws(new Exception("This exception is thrown only once")).OnlyOnce() .Returns(42); // Reads: throws, 42, 42, 42, …

Mark the last entry with .Forever() to use it for all further calls instead of starting the sequence over: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true).For(2) // Returns true the first two times .Returns(false).Forever(); // Then always returns false

Multiple Do callbacks take turns, like the entries of a Returns sequence. Mark a callback with .InParallel() to run it on every call instead: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, … call")) .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on every call")).InParallel() .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … call")); .InParallel() only applies to Do callbacks, not to Returns or Throws.

Callbacks can receive the zero-based invocation counter as their first parameter: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Do((count, type, amount) => Console.WriteLine($"Call #{count}: {amount} {type}")); dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.OnGet .Do((count, value) => Console.WriteLine($"Read #{count}, value: {value}")); // Indexer setter: the counter, then the key(s), then the new value dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].OnSet .Do((count, type, newValue) => Console.WriteLine($"Set #{count}: this[{type}] = {newValue}"));

VerifyThatAllInteractionsAreVerified() returns true when every recorded interaction was matched by at least one verification. Use it to make sure that the code under test made no calls you didn't expect: dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1).Once(); bool allVerified = dispenser.Mock.VerifyThatAllInteractionsAreVerified(); await That(allVerified).IsTrue();

VerifyThatAllSetupsAreUsed() returns true when every setup was matched by at least one interaction. Use it to make sure that your test setup and the test execution match: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Milk", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); bool allUsed = dispenser.Mock.VerifyThatAllSetupsAreUsed(); await That(allUsed).IsFalse().Because("the \"Milk\" setup was not used"); note Both methods return a bool instead of throwing, so assert the result with your assertion library.

A mock records all interactions from the moment it is created. To only verify the interactions within a given scope, use a monitor: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); MockMonitor<Mock.IMockVerifyForIChocolateDispenser> monitor = dispenser.Mock.Monitor(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // Not monitored using (monitor.Run()) { dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 2); // Monitored } dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 3); // Not monitored // Verifications on the monitor only count the interactions while it was running monitor.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); MockMonitor<T> lives in the Mockolate.Monitor namespace. You can call monitor.Run() multiple times; each run adds to the monitored interactions.

For simpler scenarios, you can clear all recorded interactions of a mock with ClearAllInteractions(): IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // Clears all previously recorded interactions dispenser.Mock.ClearAllInteractions(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 2); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); Setups are not affected by ClearAllInteractions().

Class mocks can also set up and verify protected virtual and abstract members. They work like public members, but are reached through Mock.SetupProtected, Mock.RaiseProtected and Mock.VerifyProtected: public abstract class ChocolateDispenser { protected virtual bool DispenseInternal(string type, int amount) => true; protected virtual int InternalStock { get; set; } protected virtual int this[int slot] { get => 0; set { } } } ChocolateDispenser dispenser = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock();

// Set up a protected method dispenser.Mock.SetupProtected.DispenseInternal("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true); // Set up a protected property dispenser.Mock.SetupProtected.InternalStock.InitializeWith(100); All setup options of methods, properties and indexers are available.

// A protected method was called dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected.DispenseInternal("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // A protected property was read and set dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected.InternalStock.Got().AtLeastOnce(); dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected.InternalStock.Set(100).Once(); // A protected indexer was read and set dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected[0].Got().Once(); dispenser.Mock.VerifyProtected[0].Set(42).Once(); All verification options work the same as for public members.

Scenarios let you define multiple sets of setups on a single mock and switch between them at runtime. This is useful when the collaborator behaves differently depending on its internal state, for example a chocolate dispenser that starts empty, becomes loaded after Refill(…), and runs out of stock after dispensing. The examples on this page add a Refill method to the IChocolateDispenser and use an OutOfStockException: public interface IChocolateDispenser { // the members from the core concepts, and: bool Refill(int amount); } public class OutOfStockException : Exception; A mock always has an active scenario (the empty string "" by default). When a member is called, Mockolate looks for a matching setup in the active scenario first, and then in the default setups.

Use InScenario(name) to scope setups to a named scenario. Its Setup property mirrors dispenser.Mock.Setup, but the setups only apply while the scenario is active: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("empty").Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Throws<OutOfStockException>(); dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded").Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true); A callback overload groups multiple setups of the same scenario: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded", scope => { scope.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); scope.Setup.Refill(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); });

Chain .TransitionTo(name) on any method, property, indexer or event subscription setup to change the active scenario whenever the setup is used. The transition happens in addition to the return value or exception of the setup: dispenser.Mock.InScenario("empty") .Setup.Refill(It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .TransitionTo("loaded"); dispenser.Mock.InScenario("loaded") .Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .TransitionTo("empty"); To set the starting state, change the active scenario directly with dispenser.Mock.TransitionTo("empty");.

When the mock is called, Mockolate looks for a matching setup in this order: The setups of the active scenario. The default setups (registered via dispenser.Mock.Setup). The mock's default behavior. Scenario setups add to the default setups instead of replacing them: register catch-all setups in the default scope and override specific members per scenario. Setups registered via InScenario never apply outside their scenario.

.NET 8 or later Static interface members can be mocked on .NET 8 or later. Mockolate supports mocking static abstract and static virtual members of interfaces. They are set up, raised and verified like instance members, but through Mock.SetupStatic, Mock.RaiseStatic and Mock.VerifyStatic. C# only allows calls to static abstract members through a generic type parameter that is constrained to the interface, so code that uses them typically looks like this: public interface IChocolateFactory { static abstract string DefaultRecipe { get; set; } static abstract int ProduceBatch(string type, int amount); static abstract event Action<int> BatchCompleted; } public static class ChocolateProduction { public static string ReadRecipe<TFactory>() where TFactory : IChocolateFactory => TFactory.DefaultRecipe; public static int Produce<TFactory>(string type, int amount) where TFactory : IChocolateFactory => TFactory.ProduceBatch(type, amount); public static void Subscribe<TFactory>(Action<int> handler) where TFactory : IChocolateFactory => TFactory.BatchCompleted += handler; } In the test, create the mock as usual and pass the generated mock type Mock.IChocolateFactory as the type argument: IChocolateFactory factory = IChocolateFactory.CreateMock(); // Set up static members factory.Mock.SetupStatic.ProduceBatch("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(42); factory.Mock.SetupStatic.DefaultRecipe.Returns("Dark"); // Call them through the generated mock type string recipe = ChocolateProduction.ReadRecipe<Mock.IChocolateFactory>(); int produced = ChocolateProduction.Produce<Mock.IChocolateFactory>("Dark", 10); ChocolateProduction.Subscribe<Mock.IChocolateFactory>(amount => Console.WriteLine($"Batch of {amount} ready")); await That(recipe).IsEqualTo("Dark"); await That(produced).IsEqualTo(42); // Raise static events factory.Mock.RaiseStatic.BatchCompleted(produced); // Verify static interactions factory.Mock.VerifyStatic.ProduceBatch("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); factory.Mock.VerifyStatic.DefaultRecipe.Got().Once(); factory.Mock.VerifyStatic.BatchCompleted.Subscribed().Once();

Static calls are routed to the mock that was created last in the current async flow (internally an AsyncLocal). Tests that run in parallel therefore don't interfere with each other. warning Within a single test, create at most one mock per interface with static members. When you create a second mock of the same interface, all static calls are routed to the second mock.
Mockolate ships with Roslyn analyzers and code fixes that catch mistakes at compile time. They are part of the Mockolate package, so there is nothing to install.

A verification without a count assertion. Verify methods only return a VerificationResult and do not throw on their own. You have to specify how often you expect the call to happen, e.g. .AtLeastOnce() or .Exactly(n), or use the verification result in another way. IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); // Mockolate0001: Add a count assertion like .AtLeastOnce() or use the result. dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()); The included code fix adds the .AtLeastOnce() count assertion: dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).AtLeastOnce();

A type that cannot be mocked. This rule prevents you from mocking unsupported types: CreateMock(): the type must be an interface, a delegate or a class that can be derived from (e.g. not sealed). Implementing<T>(): the type must be an interface. It also fires when the type has a member that the mock would have to implement (an abstract member, or an interface member without a default implementation), but that your assembly cannot access: for example an internal abstract or private protected abstract member, or a { get; internal set; } property, on a type from a referenced assembly that does not grant InternalsVisibleTo. There is no valid code a mock could emit for such a member, so the type cannot be mocked at all. When a derived type already implements the inaccessible member The rule only considers members that the mock still has to implement. If a more derived type in the referenced assembly already overrides the inaccessible member, that type stays mockable: // In a referenced assembly that does not grant InternalsVisibleTo: public abstract class Dispenser { internal abstract void Refill(); } public abstract class ChocolateDispenser : Dispenser { internal override void Refill() { } } // Mockolate0002 fires for Dispenser, but ChocolateDispenser mocks fine. ChocolateDispenser dispenser = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); Refill itself is not part of the mock, since your assembly cannot see it. An internal abstract override re-declaration does not count as an implementation, so the rule still fires for it. The same applies per accessor. For a property such as public abstract string Flavor { get; internal set; }, an override further down that implements the setter makes the type mockable. The mock then overrides the getter only, and Setup and Verify only offer the getter, since writes never reach the mock. See properties with only one accessor and indexers with only one accessor.

A member with a ref struct that Mockolate cannot set up. The mock still compiles and everything else on the type stays mockable, but the reported member gets no Setup or Verify members, and calling it throws a NotSupportedException. The rule fires in two situations. 1. The project does not meet the requirements for ref struct parameters Custom ref struct parameters (anything other than Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>) need a target framework of .NET 9 or later and C# 13 or later. Upgrade the target framework or <LangVersion> to resolve the warning. 2. The member uses a ref struct in a position that is never supported A method or delegate that returns a custom ref struct, a property of a custom ref struct type, or an indexer whose value is a custom ref struct. A delegate with a custom ref struct parameter, or with a ref readonly Span<T> / ref readonly ReadOnlySpan<T> parameter. Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> are supported everywhere else, both as parameters and as values. Virtual members of class mocks are not reported A virtual member of a mocked class keeps working: the mock forwards the call to the wrapped instance, or to the base class implementation, so there is nothing to fix. The forwarded call ignores the MockBehavior settings, because there is no setup to apply them to, and it is not recorded. Interface members, abstract members, init accessors and ref-returning methods have nothing to forward to. These are the ones the warning reports. See Ref struct parameters for the supported features.

With union parameters, a collection expression, a target-typed new(…) or a value that relies on a user-defined implicit conversion does not compile as a Setup or Verify argument (CS1503, CS1729 or CS9174). The included code fix adds the parameter type: // CS1729: 'ParameterArg<TimeSpan>' does not contain a constructor that takes 3 arguments timer.Mock.Setup.Wait(new(0, 0, 5)); // after the code fix timer.Mock.Setup.Wait(new TimeSpan(0, 0, 5));

Mockolate v4 supports .NET 11 and C# 15: with C# 15, the setup and verify methods take a value, a matcher or a predicate in the same parameter, so predicates no longer need It.Satisfies. This page covers what you need to know to upgrade. The complete list of changes, pull request by pull request, is in the GitHub releases. To upgrade: Update Mockolate to 4.x and fix the new Mockolate0001 warnings. If your test project compiles with C# 15, e.g. because it targets net11.0, fix the compile errors with the code fix and review the changes the compiler does not catch. Run your tests. A test project below C# 15 keeps the setup and verify methods of v3, so only the first step applies to it. Keep the v3 methods Set <MockolateUnionParameters>false</MockolateUnionParameters> in the project file to keep the setup and verify methods of v3 on any compiler, e.g. to retarget to .NET 11 first and switch to the new methods later.

These changes compile unchanged with C# 15, but an existing test may now check something different than before: null for an optional value type parameter. For a non-nullable value type parameter with a declared default value, null and default match default(T), not the declared default. Leave out the argument to match the declared default value. Delegate parameters. For a parameter whose type is a delegate, a lambda is matched as a value, not as a predicate. For an object parameter, a lambda literal is a predicate, while a delegate stored in a variable is a value. See union parameter semantics.
documents.s: Changes the compiler does not catch

documents.t: Mockolate0001 now also reports an unused verification with only values, such as Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1), and one without parameters, such as Verify.Restock(). Such a statement asserts nothing, so a build that treats warnings as errors fails where it was silently passing before. The included code fix adds the .AtLeastOnce() count assertion.

When the test project compiles with C# 15, every value-capable parameter of a setup or verify method takes a value or an It matcher, and an overload takes a predicate: - dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.Satisfies<string>(type => type.StartsWith("D")), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); + dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(type => type.StartsWith("D"), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); It.Satisfies keeps working. Overloaded methods, generic methods, params methods, members with custom ref struct parameters and some indexers keep the methods of v3; see union parameters for the complete list.

A union-typed parameter does not pass its type on to the argument, so a collection expression, a target-typed new(…) or a value that relies on a user-defined implicit conversion no longer compiles (CS1503, CS1729 or CS9174). The included code fix adds the type: - timer.Mock.Setup.Wait(new(0, 0, 5)); + timer.Mock.Setup.Wait(new TimeSpan(0, 0, 5)); You can also name the type in a matcher, e.g. It.Is<TimeSpan>(new(0, 0, 5)).
documents.s: Arguments that need an explicit type

documents.t: The generated ParameterArg<T> type relies on UnionAttribute, OverloadResolutionPriorityAttribute and CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute, and Mockolate declares those the compilation lacks. If another generator such as PolySharp declares them too, set <MockolateUnionAttributePolyfills>false</MockolateUnionAttributePolyfills>. See union parameters.
IMockBehaviorInitializer: the empty marker interface in the Mockolate.Behavior namespace was never used by Mockolate and is removed. Remove any implementation of it; it had no effect.

These additions need no change in your code. .NET 11: Mockolate targets net11.0. Predicates as arguments: with C# 15, setup and verify methods take a predicate directly, see union parameters. Extern aliases: types from a reference with an extern alias can be mocked.

A test usually checks one class, the system under test (SUT). The SUT talks to collaborators such as a database, a web service or a hardware device. A mock replaces such a collaborator: it implements the same interface (or derives from the same class), lets you decide what it returns, and records how it was called. Throughout this documentation the examples use this collaborator: public delegate void ChocolateDispensedDelegate(string type, int amount); public interface IChocolateDispenser { int this[string type] { get; set; } int TotalDispensed { get; set; } bool Dispense(string type, int amount); event ChocolateDispensedDelegate ChocolateDispensed; } The mock is called dispenser, and the class that uses it is called sut: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); VendingMachine sut = new VendingMachine(dispenser); Pages that need further members declare them next to the example.
documents.s: Mocks and the system under test

documents.t: The source generator adds a CreateMock() method to every type you mock. The returned object is an IChocolateDispenser, so you can pass it to your code directly. Everything that configures or inspects the mock is reached through its Mock property: Member Purpose Mock.Setup Decide how methods, properties and indexers behave. See Setup. Mock.Raise Raise events on the mock. See Events. Mock.Verify Check how the mock was used. See Verify interactions. Mock.SetupProtected, Mock.VerifyProtected, … The same for protected members of class mocks. See Protected members. Mock.SetupStatic, Mock.VerifyStatic, … The same for static interface members. See Static interface members. Mock.InScenario(…), Mock.TransitionTo(…) Switch between sets of setups. See Scenarios. Mock.Monitor(), Mock.ClearAllInteractions() Limit which interactions are counted. See Monitor interactions. Mock.As<T>() Reach an additional interface. See Create mocks. The generated setup and verification members mirror the members of the mocked type, so a typo or a wrong argument type is a compile error instead of a runtime exception.

Each call to the mock goes through the same steps: The call is recorded, so that you can verify it later. Mockolate looks for a matching setup. A setup matches when every argument satisfies its parameter matcher. If several setups match, the one defined last wins. The setup's callbacks run, and its return value or exception is used. Without a matching setup, the mock falls back to its MockBehavior: methods return a default value: false, 0, an empty string, an empty collection, a completed task, or null for other reference types; properties and indexers behave like normal storage: reading returns the value that was last written, or the default value if nothing was written yet; a mock created with ThrowingWhenNotSetup() throws a MockNotSetupException instead. dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("White", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(false); bool dark = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); bool white = dispenser.Dispense("White", 1); await That(dark).IsTrue().Because("only the first setup matches"); await That(white).IsFalse().Because("both setups match and the later one wins"); int before = dispenser.TotalDispensed; dispenser.TotalDispensed = 5; int after = dispenser.TotalDispensed; await That(before).IsEqualTo(0).Because("nothing was written yet"); await That(after).IsEqualTo(5).Because("the property stores the written value"); tip Define general setups first and more specific ones afterwards. Because the last matching setup wins, every dispenser.Mock.Setup.X statement starts a new setup that replaces earlier ones with the same arguments. Configure one setup by chaining: // ✔️ One setup: the property starts at 42 and logs every write dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .InitializeWith(42) .OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine(newValue)); // ❌ Two setups: the second one replaces the first, so the property starts at 0 dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(42); dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine(newValue)); Class mocks A class mock also calls the base class implementation of a virtual member, even when a setup matches. The setup's return value takes precedence; the base class result is used only when no setup provides one. Use SkippingBaseClass() to turn the base class calls off.
documents.s: What happens when the mock is called

documents.t: Verifications count the recorded interactions that match the given arguments and compare the count with your expectation. Nothing is checked until you call a count method such as .Once(), .Never() or .AtLeast(2); the Mockolate0001 analyzer warns you when you forget it. dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // passes dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Milk", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); // throws a MockVerificationException The exception message describes the expectation and what actually happened: Failure message Expected that mock invoked method Dispense("Milk", It.IsAny<int>()) exactly once, but it never did. Setups and verifications are independent: you can verify calls that have no setup, and a setup does not expect to be called. To check that every setup was used or every interaction was verified, see Check for unexpected interactions.
A complete example combines these concepts in one end-to-end test. The cheat sheet lists the most common calls on one page.
The most common calls at a glance. Follow the links for details. using Mockolate; using Mockolate.Verify;

IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); IChocolateDispenser strict = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); ChocolateDispenser classMock = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(["constructor", "arguments"]); IChocolateDispenser spy = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock().Wrapping(realDispenser); IChocolateDispenser multi = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock().Implementing<ILemonadeDispenser>();

Each line is an alternative: a later setup with the same arguments replaces an earlier one, so chain everything that belongs to one setup. dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns((type, amount) => amount < 10); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Green", It.IsAny<int>()).Throws<InvalidOperationException>(); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true).Returns(false); // sequence, repeats dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true).Returns(false).Forever(); // then always false dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Do((type, amount) => Console.WriteLine(amount)); dispenser.Mock.Setup.DispenseAsync("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).ReturnsAsync(3); // for Task<int> methods

dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(42); // behaves like a property, starting at 42 dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.Returns(42); // always returns 42 dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(42).OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine(newValue)); dispenser.Mock.Setup["Dark"].InitializeWith(10); dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].Returns(type => type.Length);
dispenser.Mock.Raise.ChocolateDispensed("Dark", 3);

Matcher Matches "Dark" or It.Is("Dark") an equal value It.IsAny<int>() any value It.Satisfies<int>(x => x > 0) values that satisfy the predicate It.IsOneOf("Dark", "Milk") one of the values It.IsInRange(1, 10) a value in the range It.IsNull<string>(), It.IsNotNull<string>() null, anything but null It.Matches("Da*") a wildcard pattern It.Contains(5), It.SequenceEquals(1, 2) collections It.IsOut(() => 42), It.IsRef<int>(v => v + 1) out and ref parameters Match.AnyParameters() any combination of parameters

dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Once(); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Never(); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).AtLeast(2); dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Got().AtLeastOnce(); dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Set(42).Once(); dispenser.Mock.Verify["Dark"].Got().Twice(); dispenser.Mock.Verify.ChocolateDispensed.Subscribed().Once(); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1).Then(m => m.Dispense("Milk", 2)); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)).Once();

The following example combines indexers, methods, events, stateful setup and verification into a single end-to-end scenario. The dispenser keeps track of its stock in the indexer, and every successful Dispense call reduces the stock and raises the ChocolateDispensed event: using Mockolate; using Mockolate.Verify; using static aweXpect.Expect; public delegate void ChocolateDispensedDelegate(string type, int amount); public interface IChocolateDispenser { int this[string type] { get; set; } int TotalDispensed { get; set; } bool Dispense(string type, int amount); event ChocolateDispensedDelegate ChocolateDispensed; } // Create a mock of IChocolateDispenser IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); // Setup: initial stock of 10 for Dark chocolate dispenser.Mock.Setup["Dark"].InitializeWith(10); // Setup: Dispense decreases the stock if there is enough, and returns true/false dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns((type, amount) => { int current = dispenser[type]; if (current >= amount) { dispenser[type] = current - amount; dispenser.Mock.Raise.ChocolateDispensed(type, amount); return true; } return false; }); // Track the dispensed amount via the event int dispensedAmount = 0; dispenser.ChocolateDispensed += (type, amount) => { dispensedAmount += amount; }; // Act: try to dispense chocolates bool gotChoc1 = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 4); bool gotChoc2 = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 5); bool gotChoc3 = dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 6); // Assert: check the results and the interactions await That(gotChoc1).IsTrue(); await That(gotChoc2).IsTrue(); await That(gotChoc3).IsFalse().Because("only 1 Dark chocolate is left"); await That(dispensedAmount).IsEqualTo(9); await That(dispenser["Dark"]).IsEqualTo(1); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Exactly(3); dispenser.Mock.Verify["Dark"].Set(It.IsAny<int>()).Twice(); The individual features are described in detail on the following pages: Create mocks Setup of methods, properties, indexers and events Parameter matching Verify interactions

You can create mocks of interfaces, classes and delegates. The source generator adds a static CreateMock() method to every type you mock. Example types used on this page Besides IChocolateDispenser, this page uses: public abstract class ChocolateDispenser { public abstract bool Dispense(string type, int amount); } public class MyChocolateDispenser : IChocolateDispenser { // a real implementation of IChocolateDispenser } public interface ILemonadeDispenser { bool DispenseLemonade(int amount); } // Create a mock of an interface IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); // Create a mock of a class ChocolateDispenser classMock = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); For classes without a parameterless constructor, pass the constructor arguments as an array: public abstract class ChocolateDispenserWithCtor(string defaultType, int capacity) { public abstract bool Dispense(string type, int amount); } ChocolateDispenserWithCtor classMock = ChocolateDispenserWithCtor.CreateMock(["Dark", 42]); note A class mock overrides the virtual and abstract members of the class. Non-virtual members cannot be intercepted and always run the real implementation. Sealed classes cannot be mocked; the Mockolate0002 analyzer reports this at compile time.

You can pass the setups directly to CreateMock. These setups are applied before the constructor of a class mock runs, so they also apply to virtual members that the constructor calls: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(setup => { setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(0); }); The setup callback can be combined with a MockBehavior and with constructor arguments in the same call.

A MockBehavior controls what the mock does when no setup matches. MockBehavior.Default returns default values and calls the base class implementation of class mocks (see Core concepts). Change it with the fluent -ing methods: // Throw a MockNotSetupException for every call without a matching setup IChocolateDispenser strictMock = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); // Combine a behavior with constructor arguments MockBehavior behavior = MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup(); ChocolateDispenserWithCtor classMock = ChocolateDispenserWithCtor.CreateMock(behavior, ["Dark", 42]); MockBehavior is an immutable record, so every method returns a new instance and you can safely share one behavior between many mocks and tests: MockBehavior strict = MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup(); IChocolateDispenser dispenser1 = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(strict); ILemonadeDispenser dispenser2 = ILemonadeDispenser.CreateMock(strict); Option Default Purpose ThrowingWhenNotSetup() off Throws a MockNotSetupException when no matching setup is found, instead of returning a default value. SkippingBaseClass() off Class mocks no longer call the base class implementation; without a setup they return a default value instead. SkippingInteractionRecording() off Interactions are not recorded. Setups, return values, callbacks and base class calls still work, but every verification throws a MockException. Useful in performance-sensitive scenarios. WithDefaultValueFor<T>(…) sensible defaults Customizes the default value for type T (see below). Initialize<T>(…) - Applies the given setups to every mock of type T created with this behavior. UseConstructorParametersFor<T>(…) - Default constructor arguments for mocks of class T, used unless you pass explicit arguments to CreateMock([…]). The Func<object?[]> overload creates them anew for each mock.

When no setup matches, the mock returns: an empty collection for collection types (e.g. IEnumerable<T>, List<T>), an empty string for string, a completed task for Task, Task<T>, ValueTask and ValueTask<T>, a tuple with recursively defaulted values for tuples, default(T) for value types and null for other reference types. You can register custom factories per type using .WithDefaultValueFor<T>(): MockBehavior behavior = MockBehavior.Default .WithDefaultValueFor<string>(() => "default") .WithDefaultValueFor<int>(() => 42); IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(behavior); For full control, implement IDefaultValueGenerator and pass it to the MockBehavior(IDefaultValueGenerator) constructor.

Use .Implementing<T>() to create a mock that also implements further interfaces: // A ChocolateDispenser that also implements ILemonadeDispenser ChocolateDispenser dispenser = ChocolateDispenser.CreateMock().Implementing<ILemonadeDispenser>(); // With setups for the additional interface IChocolateDispenser dispenser2 = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock() .Implementing<ILemonadeDispenser>(setup => setup.DispenseLemonade(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true)); Use Mock.As<T>() to reach the Setup and Verify members of the additional interface: dispenser.Mock.As<ILemonadeDispenser>().Setup.DispenseLemonade(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.As<ILemonadeDispenser>().Verify.DispenseLemonade(5).Once(); When the mock is already typed as the additional interface, its own Mock property reaches the same members, so you can skip As<T>(): ((ILemonadeDispenser)dispenser).Mock.Setup.DispenseLemonade(It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); All interfaces share the same mock: recorded interactions, scenario state and setups apply to every view of it. warning .Implementing<T>() returns a new mock instead of changing the one it was called on. Keep the returned reference; the original one does not implement T. Only the first type can be a class; additional types must be interfaces. Mock.As<T>() throws a MockException when the mock does not implement T, for example because it was not created with .Implementing<T>(). On class mocks, .Implementing<T>() reuses the constructor arguments the mock was created with. When the class already implements the interface .Implementing<T>() is also useful when the mocked class itself implements T, because it makes non-virtual members that the class implements mockable through the interface: public interface ICalculator { int Add(int a, int b); int Multiply(int a, int b); } public abstract class Calculator : ICalculator { public int Add(int a, int b) => a + b; // not virtual public abstract int Multiply(int a, int b); } Calculator calculator = Calculator.CreateMock().Implementing<ICalculator>(); // `Multiply` is overridable, so the class and the interface share one member: // either surface configures it, and both calls are recorded against it. calculator.Mock.Setup.Multiply(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(7); int viaClass = calculator.Multiply(3, 4); int viaInterface = ((ICalculator)calculator).Multiply(3, 4); await That(viaClass).IsEqualTo(7); await That(viaInterface).IsEqualTo(7); // `Add` is not virtual, so only the call through the interface can be intercepted. calculator.Mock.As<ICalculator>().Setup.Add(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(99); int addViaClass = calculator.Add(1, 2); int addViaInterface = ((ICalculator)calculator).Add(1, 2); await That(addViaClass).IsEqualTo(3).Because("the class call runs the real implementation"); await That(addViaInterface).IsEqualTo(99); Members hidden with new Mock.As<T>() also reaches a base interface whose members the mocked interface hides with new. No .Implementing<T>() is needed, because the base interface is already part of the mocked type. Methods, properties and events stay separate members, each with its own setups and recorded interactions: public interface IChocolateShelfBase { int Restock(); } public interface IChocolateShelf : IChocolateShelfBase { new int Restock(); } IChocolateShelf shelf = IChocolateShelf.CreateMock(); shelf.Mock.Setup.Restock().Returns(42); shelf.Mock.As<IChocolateShelfBase>().Setup.Restock().Returns(43); int viaDerived = shelf.Restock(); int viaBase = ((IChocolateShelfBase)shelf).Restock(); await That(viaDerived).IsEqualTo(42); await That(viaBase).IsEqualTo(43); shelf.Mock.Verify.Restock().Once(); shelf.Mock.As<IChocolateShelfBase>().Verify.Restock().Once(); Indexers are the exception: they are keyed by their parameter signature rather than by the declaring interface, so a new indexer and the base indexer it hides share the same storage.

Use .Wrapping(instance) to forward all calls to a real object while still recording them, like a spy: MyChocolateDispenser realDispenser = new MyChocolateDispenser(); IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock().Wrapping(realDispenser); // The call is forwarded to the real instance dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 5); // You can still verify interactions dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5).Once(); Both interface and class types can be wrapped. Setups take precedence over the wrapped instance, so you can still override individual members. Interface members are forwarded through the interface that declares them. This also covers members that hide a base member with new, and same-named members declared by several base interfaces. Protected members are not forwarded; the base class implementation is used instead. Init-only properties are not forwarded, since the wrapped instance is already constructed.

.NET 10 SDK and C# 14 Mockolate generates its mocks with C# 14 extension members, so you need the .NET 10 SDK to build your tests. If your test project pins <LangVersion>, it must be 14 or later (or latest). Your test projects can still target any supported framework: .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 8, .NET 10 or .NET Framework 4.8.

Suppose your code depends on a chocolate dispenser: Production code public interface IChocolateDispenser { bool Dispense(string type, int amount); } public class VendingMachine(IChocolateDispenser dispenser) { public string Buy(string type, int amount) => dispenser.Dispense(type, amount) ? "Enjoy!" : "Sold out"; } To test VendingMachine without a real dispenser, create a mock of IChocolateDispenser, tell it how to behave, and check afterwards how it was used: VendingMachineTests.cs using Mockolate; using Mockolate.Verify; using static aweXpect.Expect; public class VendingMachineTests { [Test] public async Task Buy_WhenChocolateIsAvailable_ShouldDispenseIt() { IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); VendingMachine sut = new VendingMachine(dispenser); string result = sut.Buy("Dark", 4); await That(result).IsEqualTo("Enjoy!"); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 4).Once(); } } CreateMock() is generated for every type you mock, so IntelliSense shows it as soon as you type IChocolateDispenser.. Every mock has a Mock property that gives access to Setup, Verify and Raise. It.IsAny<int>() is a parameter matcher. Plain values like "Dark" match by equality. .Once() throws a MockVerificationException when the call count does not match. It lives in the Mockolate.Verify namespace. aweXpect in the examples The test uses TUnit, and the examples in this documentation check results with aweXpect (await That(...)). aweXpect is optional: Mockolate works with any test framework and assertion library. If you use aweXpect, the aweXpect.Mockolate extension also lets you write verifications as awaitable expectations: await That(dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 4)).Once();.

Core concepts explains how mocks, setups and verifications fit together. A complete example combines properties, indexers, events and methods in one test. The cheat sheet lists the most common calls on one page.

Coming from Moq, NSubstitute or FakeItEasy? There are two ways to move your tests over: Automatically: for Moq and NSubstitute, the Mockolate.Migration package reports every mock it can migrate and rewrites it with a code fix. By hand: this page shows the same test in each library and translates the most common calls. Select the library you know; the choice applies to all examples on this page.

All examples use this interface: public delegate void ChocolateDispensedDelegate(string type, int amount); public interface IChocolateDispenser { int this[string type] { get; set; } int TotalDispensed { get; set; } bool Dispense(string type, int amount); event ChocolateDispensedDelegate ChocolateDispensed; } Moq NSubstitute FakeItEasy Moq // Setup Mock<IChocolateDispenser> mock = new Mock<IChocolateDispenser>(); mock.Setup(x => x.Dispense("Dark", 2)).Returns(true); mock.SetupGet(x => x["Dark"]).Returns(10); // Usage int available = mock.Object["Dark"]; bool success = mock.Object.Dispense("Dark", 2); mock.Raise(m => m.ChocolateDispensed += null, "Dark", 2); // Verification mock.Verify(x => x.Dispense("Dark", 2), Times.Once()); mock.VerifyGet(x => x["Dark"], Times.Once()); NSubstitute // Setup IChocolateDispenser substitute = Substitute.For<IChocolateDispenser>(); substitute.Dispense("Dark", 2).Returns(true); substitute["Dark"].Returns(10); // Usage int available = substitute["Dark"]; bool success = substitute.Dispense("Dark", 2); substitute.ChocolateDispensed += Raise.Event<ChocolateDispensedDelegate>("Dark", 2); The Mockolate.Migration package contains a Roslyn analyzer and code fixes that migrate Moq and NSubstitute mocks to Mockolate. The analyzer reports every mock it can migrate, and the code fix rewrites the whole mock in one step: the construction, all its setups and verifications, the event wiring and, for Moq, every .Object access. Diagnostic Source library Code fix title MockolateM001 Moq Migrate Moq to Mockolate MockolateM002 NSubstitute Migrate NSubstitute to Mockolate

Install the package into the test project you want to migrate, next to Mockolate itself: .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Mockolate.Migration <PackageReference Include="Mockolate.Migration" Version="0.6.0" PrivateAssets="all" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Mockolate.Migration" Version="0.6.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Mockolate.Migration" PrivateAssets="all" /> Latest version: 0.6.0 The package contains only the analyzer and the code fixes, no runtime code. You need it only while you migrate: once a project no longer uses Moq or NSubstitute, remove the reference again.

After you install the package, each mock that can be migrated is reported as a warning (MockolateM001 or MockolateM002). Apply the code fix in your IDE (Visual Studio, Rider or VS Code with C# Dev Kit). To migrate many mocks at once, use Fix all occurrences for the document, project or solution, or run the code fix from the command line: dotnet format analyzers --diagnostics MockolateM001 MockolateM002 Then build, run your tests and check the cases that need manual review. What the code fix rewrites, with examples and the supported constructs, is described per source library: Migrating from Moq Migrating from NSubstitute

The code fix leaves a // TODO(MockolateM001) or // TODO(MockolateM002) comment where it cannot finish the migration on its own. Search for them after you apply the fix: Nested mocks: Moq and NSubstitute create mocks for nested members (m => m.Child.Prop) automatically. Mockolate does not, so set up the parent to return a mock for Child yourself. CallInfo callbacks that cannot be rewritten safely, for example when they use call directly, compute the index at runtime, assign out or ref arguments, call an ambiguous call.Arg<T>(), or declare local variables with the same names as the parameters of the method. The code fix does not mark these cases: Call order: the code fix removes Moq's InSequence(…) wrapper from the setups. Mockolate checks the order after the calls instead: add a Then(…) chain to the verification. Constructs that are not in the tables of supported Moq and NSubstitute constructs, for example Moq's Verifiable(), VerifyAll(), Protected(), As<T>() or Mock.Of<T>(), and NSubstitute's Arg.Do<T>(…), Received.InOrder(…) or Configure(). Rewrite them by hand; the translation table shows the Mockolate equivalents.

The MockolateM001 code fix rewrites new Mock<T>(…) to T.CreateMock(…), changes the declared type from Mock<T> to T, drops every .Object access and moves setups and verifications to Mock.Setup and Mock.Verify. The examples use the IChocolateDispenser interface from the migration overview and the VendingMachine from Getting started. The code fix keeps your variable names, so the mock keeps its name and sut stays the system under test. The MockolateM002 code fix rewrites Substitute.For<T>(…) to T.CreateMock(…) and moves the setups (substitute.Method(args).Returns(…)) and verifications (substitute.Received().Method(…)) to Mock.Setup and Mock.Verify. The examples use the IChocolateDispenser interface from the migration overview and the VendingMachine from Getting started. The code fix keeps your variable names, so the mock keeps its name and sut stays the system under test. In NSubstitute, the callbacks of Returns(call => …), When(…).Do(call => …) and AndDoes(call => …) receive a CallInfo with the arguments of the call. The Mockolate callbacks take the parameters of the method instead, so the code fix rewrites the lambda: If the lambda does not use call, the parameter is dropped: Do(call => count++) becomes Do(() => count++). If the lambda only reads arguments at a constant position (call.ArgAt<T>(0), call[0]) or by a unique type (call.Arg<T>()), it gets the parameters of the method, and each access is replaced with the parameter: Returns(call => call.ArgAt<int>(1) > 0) becomes Returns((string type, int amount) => amount > 0). Otherwise the lambda is kept as it is and marked with a // TODO comment. See what needs manual review.
