Setups and verifications take one argument per parameter of the mocked member. Each argument decides which calls the setup applies to, or which calls the verification counts. You can pass: a value, which matches by equality (the same as It.Is(value)), or a matcher from the It class, such as It.IsAny<int>(). dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(It.IsOneOf("Dark", "Milk"), It.IsInRange(1, 5)).AtLeastOnce(); The same matchers work everywhere: in method and indexer setups, in verifications, and for delegates. Example types used on this page Besides IChocolateDispenser, this page uses: public interface IChocolateKitchen { int Process(string recipe); bool ValidateEmail(string email); bool TryParse(string input, out int amount); bool Increment(ref int value); bool Fill(IEnumerable<int> amounts); bool Pack(IList<string> types); bool SetTemperature(double celsius); bool Scan(Span<byte> data); } IChocolateKitchen kitchen = IChocolateKitchen.CreateMock();

Matcher Matches It.IsAny<T>() any value of type T It.Is<T>(value) a value equal to value It.IsNot<T>(value) any value not equal to value It.IsOneOf<T>(params values) any of the given values It.IsNotOneOf<T>(params values) any value that is not one of the given values It.IsNull<T>() null It.IsNotNull<T>() any value except null It.IsTrue() / It.IsFalse() true / false It.IsInRange(min, max) a value between min and max (inclusive); append .Exclusive() to exclude both bounds It.Satisfies<T>(predicate) any value for which the predicate returns true dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.Satisfies<string>(type => type.StartsWith("D")), It.IsInRange(1, 10).Exclusive()) .Returns(true); Mixing values and matchers For members with up to 4 parameters, you can freely mix values and matchers in any position. For members with more parameters, Mockolate limits the combinations to avoid an explosion of generated overloads: either pass values for all parameters, or use matchers for all of them (wrap a value in It.Is(value)). With union parameters, values and matchers mix freely for any number of parameters. Direct predicates are only offered for members with up to 4 parameters; above that, use It.Satisfies.

Use .Using(IEqualityComparer<T>) on It.Is(), It.IsOneOf(), It.Contains() or It.SequenceEquals() to provide a custom equality comparison: kitchen.Mock.Setup.Process(It.Is("hello").Using(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) .Returns(42); int result = kitchen.Process("HELLO"); await That(result).IsEqualTo(42);

Use .Within(tolerance) on It.Is() to accept values that differ from the expected value by at most the given tolerance. It is available for double, float and decimal (numeric tolerance) as well as DateTime, DateTimeOffset and TimeSpan (TimeSpan tolerance), and for their nullable counterparts: // Accept a tempering temperature that differs from 31.5 degrees by at most 0.1 kitchen.Mock.Setup.SetTemperature(It.Is(31.5).Within(0.1)) .Returns(true); bool result = kitchen.SetTemperature(31.45); await That(result).IsTrue(); Tolerance semantics The bound is inclusive, but for double and float it is subject to the usual binary representation error, so values that lie exactly on the bound may or may not match. The tolerance must not be negative (or NaN); otherwise an ArgumentOutOfRangeException is thrown. NaN and the infinities keep matching themselves, just like without a tolerance. For nullable parameters, null only matches null; a tolerance never bridges the gap between null and a value. .Within(tolerance) cannot be combined with .Using(IEqualityComparer<T>), because a custom comparer would replace the tolerance.

Matchers are covariant in their type argument: when a method declares a parameter of a base type, a matcher for a derived type only matches calls whose argument is an instance of that derived type (or a further-derived type): public abstract class Chocolate { } public class DarkChocolate : Chocolate { } public class MilkChocolate : Chocolate { } public interface IChocolateBox { bool Add(Chocolate chocolate); } IChocolateBox box = IChocolateBox.CreateMock(); box.Mock.Setup.Add(It.IsAny<DarkChocolate>()).Returns(true); bool dark = box.Add(new DarkChocolate()); bool milk = box.Add(new MilkChocolate()); await That(dark).IsTrue(); await That(milk).IsFalse().Because("no setup matches a MilkChocolate"); // Verifications are covariant too: only dark-chocolate additions are counted. box.Mock.Verify.Add(It.IsAny<DarkChocolate>()).Once();

It.Matches(pattern) matches strings with the wildcards * (any number of characters) and ? (a single character). Matching is case-insensitive by default: kitchen.Mock.Setup.Process(It.Matches("foo*")).Returns(1); // starts with "foo" kitchen.Mock.Setup.Process(It.Matches("*foo")).Returns(2); // ends with "foo" kitchen.Mock.Setup.Process(It.Matches("*foo*")).Returns(3); // contains "foo" Append .CaseSensitive() to require an exact case match, or .AsRegex() to treat the pattern as a regular expression: kitchen.Mock.Setup.Process(It.Matches("Foo*").CaseSensitive()) .Returns(1); kitchen.Mock.Setup.ValidateEmail(It.Matches(@"^\w+@\w+\.\w+$").AsRegex()) .Returns(true); // Case-sensitive regex kitchen.Mock.Setup.Process(It.Matches("^[A-Z]+$").AsRegex().CaseSensitive()) .Returns(1); To match a literal * or ?, use a regular expression and escape the text: It.Matches(Regex.Escape("a*b") + "$").AsRegex() matches strings that end with a*b.

Matcher Matches It.Contains<T>(item) a collection that contains item It.SequenceEquals<T>(params values) a collection whose elements equal values in the same order Both matchers support parameters declared as IEnumerable<T>, ICollection<T>, IList<T>, IReadOnlyCollection<T>, IReadOnlyList<T>, T[], List<T>, Queue<T> or Stack<T>. It.Contains<T> additionally supports ISet<T> and HashSet<T>; It.SequenceEquals<T> does not, because their enumeration order is not guaranteed. kitchen.Mock.Setup.Fill(It.Contains(5)) .Returns(true); kitchen.Mock.Setup.Pack(It.SequenceEquals("Dark", "Milk", "White")) .Returns(true); kitchen.Mock.Setup.Pack(It.Contains("DARK").Using(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) .Returns(true); bool filled = kitchen.Fill([1, 2, 5]); bool packed = kitchen.Pack(["Dark", "Milk", "White"]); await That(filled).IsTrue(); await That(packed).IsTrue();

Matcher In a setup It.IsOut<T>(setter) matches any out parameter and assigns the value returned by setter It.IsAnyOut<T>() matches any out parameter and assigns default(T) It.IsRef<T>(setter) matches any ref parameter and replaces its value with setter(value) It.IsRef<T>(predicate, setter) matches ref parameters that satisfy the predicate and replaces their value It.IsRef<T>(predicate) matches ref parameters that satisfy the predicate, without changing the value It.IsAnyRef<T>() matches any ref parameter, without changing the value kitchen.Mock.Setup.TryParse(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsOut(() => 42)) .Returns(true); bool success = kitchen.TryParse("abc", out int amount); await That(success).IsTrue(); await That(amount).IsEqualTo(42); kitchen.Mock.Setup.Increment(It.IsRef<int>(v => v + 1)) .Returns(true); int value = 5; kitchen.Increment(ref value); await That(value).IsEqualTo(6); In verifications, use It.IsOut<T>() and It.IsRef<T>() without arguments to match any out or ref parameter: kitchen.Mock.Verify.TryParse("abc", It.IsOut<int>()).Once();

.NET 8 or later The span matchers are available on .NET 8 or later. Matcher Matches It.IsSpan<T>(predicate) Span<T> parameters that satisfy the predicate It.IsAnySpan<T>() any Span<T> parameter It.IsReadOnlySpan<T>(predicate) ReadOnlySpan<T> parameters that satisfy the predicate It.IsAnyReadOnlySpan<T>() any ReadOnlySpan<T> parameter Spans cannot be stored, so Mockolate copies the span into an array and passes that array to the predicate: kitchen.Mock.Setup.Scan(It.IsSpan<byte>(data => data.Length > 0)) .Returns(true); Span<byte> buffer = new byte[] { 1, 2, 3 }; bool result = kitchen.Scan(buffer); await That(result).IsTrue();

.NET 9 and C# 13 or later Custom ref struct parameters need a target framework of .NET 9 or later and C# 13 or later. You can also mock members that take custom ref struct parameters (e.g. Utf8JsonReader or your own ref struct Packet), by value and as out, ref and ref readonly: Matcher Matches It.IsAnyRefStruct<T>() any ref struct value of type T It.IsRefStruct<T>(predicate) ref struct values that satisfy the predicate, evaluated at the time of the call It.IsRefStructBy<T, TKey>(projection) for indexers keyed by a ref struct: projects the key to a value that can be stored public readonly ref struct Packet(int id, ReadOnlySpan<byte> payload) { public int Id { get; } = id; public ReadOnlySpan<byte> Payload { get; } = payload; } public interface IPacketSink { void Consume(Packet packet); int TryParse(Packet packet); string this[Packet key] { get; set; } } IPacketSink sink = IPacketSink.CreateMock(); // Match on the live ref struct, including its span contents sink.Mock.Setup.Consume(It.IsRefStruct<Packet>(p => p.Payload.Length > 0 && p.Payload[0] == 0xFF)) .Throws<InvalidOperationException>(); // Return a value from a method with a ref struct parameter sink.Mock.Setup.TryParse(It.IsAnyRefStruct<Packet>()).Returns(42); // Indexer keyed by a ref struct: Returns for the getter, OnSet to observe writes sink.Mock.Setup[It.IsAnyRefStruct<Packet>()] .Returns("got") .OnSet(value => Console.WriteLine($"written: {value}")); // Correlate writes and reads by projecting the key to a storable value sink.Mock.Setup[It.IsRefStructBy<Packet, int>(p => p.Id)].Returns("fallback"); sink[new Packet(1, [])] = "written"; string a = sink[new Packet(1, [])]; string b = sink[new Packet(2, [])]; await That(a).IsEqualTo("written").Because("the key is matched by Id"); await That(b).IsEqualTo("fallback").Because("nothing was written under Id 2"); Limitations C# does not allow ref struct values in generic delegates, so members with ref struct parameters offer a narrower API: Setup: only Returns, Throws, OnSet(…) (for indexer setters) and SkippingBaseClass are available. .Do(…) and the advanced callback features (InParallel, When, For, Only, TransitionTo) are not. Verify: verifications count the calls, but cannot match on the ref struct value, because the value is not kept after the call. Use a matcher in the setup to filter at call time. Indexer storage: values written through an indexer keyed by a ref struct are not read back by the getter, unless every ref struct key uses It.IsRefStructBy<T, TKey>(projection). Members that Mockolate cannot support (for example methods that return a custom ref struct, or targets older than .NET 9) are reported by the Mockolate0003 analyzer.

When the consuming project compiles with C# 15, Mockolate generates the setup and verify overloads with union-typed parameters: every value-capable parameter becomes a ParameterArg<T>? that accepts an It matcher or a direct value, and a Func<T, bool> overload accepts a predicate. The number of overloads stays the same as before, but predicates no longer need It.Satisfies: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(type => type.StartsWith("D"), It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", amount => amount > 10).Once(); Union mode is enabled automatically once the compiler ships C# 15 and the project's effective language version is C# 15 or later. On a preview compiler, opt in with <MockolateUnionParameters>true</MockolateUnionParameters> together with <LangVersion>preview</LangVersion> in the project file; below that language version the property has no effect. false keeps the classic overloads on any compiler. Union parameter semantics null and default stand for default(T) of the parameter type. Leaving out an optional parameter stands for its declared default value. Unlike the classic overloads, null for a non-nullable value type parameter with a declared default value matches default(T), not the declared default. A union-typed parameter does not pass its type on to the argument: a collection expression, a target-typed new(…) or a value that relies on a user-defined implicit conversion needs an explicit type, for example new TimeSpan(0, 0, 5) or (ReadOnlyMemory<byte>)bytes. Alternatively, name the type in a matcher, as in It.Is<TimeSpan>(new(0, 0, 5)). A code fix adds the explicit type. A parameter whose type is a delegate offers the raw delegate instead of a predicate, so a lambda is still matched as a value. For an object parameter, a lambda literal is a predicate, while a delegate stored in a variable is a value. Within a union-typed member, ref, out and ref readonly parameters as well as Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> parameters keep their matcher slot (no predicate for that parameter); in parameters behave like by-value ones. Overloaded method names (including a generic sibling; a same-named member in another scope, whether public, protected or static, does not count), generic methods, params methods, members with custom ref struct parameters, and indexers that share their key count with another same-scope indexer keep the classic matcher/value overloads. Use It.Satisfies for predicates there. The generated ParameterArg<T> type relies on UnionAttribute, OverloadResolutionPriorityAttribute and CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute. Mockolate declares whichever of them the compilation lacks (neither the referenced frameworks nor the project itself provide it). Another generator such as PolySharp can provide them without Mockolate noticing; set <MockolateUnionAttributePolyfills>false</MockolateUnionAttributePolyfills> to declare that OverloadResolutionPriorityAttribute and CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute come from elsewhere (UnionAttribute keeps following the compilation), or list the attribute names the project provides.

For methods without overloads, the Match class lets you match all parameters together: Matcher Matches Match.AnyParameters() any combination of parameters Match.Parameters(Func<object?[], bool>) parameter combinations for which the predicate returns true dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(Match.Parameters(args => args[0] is string type && type.StartsWith("D") && args[1] is int amount && amount > 0)) .Returns(true); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(Match.AnyParameters()).Twice();

Use .Do(…) on a matcher to run a callback with the value of that parameter whenever the setup matches: int lastAmount = 0; dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>().Do(amount => lastAmount = amount)); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 42); await That(lastAmount).IsEqualTo(42);

Use .Monitor(out monitor) on a matcher to collect all values passed for that parameter and inspect them afterwards: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>().Monitor(out IParameterMonitor<int> monitor)); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 5); dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 7); await That(monitor.Values).IsEqualTo([5, 7]); IParameterMonitor<T> lives in the Mockolate.Parameters namespace.

A setup decides how a member of the mock behaves when it is called: what it returns, whether it throws, and which callbacks run. All setups start at dispenser.Mock.Setup and mirror the members of the mocked type: Member kind Example Methods dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); Properties dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(42); Indexers dispenser.Mock.Setup["Dark"].Returns(10); Events dispenser.Mock.Raise.ChocolateDispensed("Dark", 3);

All member kinds share the same vocabulary: Returns(…) / Throws(…) decide the result. Called several times, they form a sequence that starts over after the last entry. Do(…) runs a callback. For properties and indexers, use OnGet.Do(…) and OnSet.Do(…). InitializeWith(…) gives properties and indexers a start value, after which they behave like normal storage. Values and matchers such as It.IsAny<int>() decide which calls a setup applies to. See Parameter matching. Modifiers such as .For(n), .Only(n), .When(…) and .Forever() control how often an entry applies. See Advanced callback features. Chain what belongs together When several setups match a call, the one defined last wins. Every dispenser.Mock.Setup.X statement starts a new setup, so chain everything that belongs to one setup instead of repeating the statement: dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .InitializeWith(42) .OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine(newValue)); Members without a setup fall back to the mock's MockBehavior: methods return default values, and properties and indexers store the values written to them. You can also pass the setups directly to CreateMock.

Use the Raise member to trigger events declared on the mocked interface or class. The generated method has the same parameters as the event delegate: int dispensedAmount = 0; dispenser.ChocolateDispensed += (type, amount) => dispensedAmount += amount; dispenser.Mock.Raise.ChocolateDispensed("Dark", 3); dispenser.Mock.Raise.ChocolateDispensed("Milk", 2); await That(dispensedAmount).IsEqualTo(5); Only the handlers that are subscribed at the time the event is raised are called. This lets you test that your code subscribes to and unsubscribes from events correctly.

Use OnSubscribed and OnUnsubscribed to run a callback when a handler is added to or removed from an event. The callback can be parameterless or receive the handler's target and method: dispenser.Mock.Setup.ChocolateDispensed.OnSubscribed .Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Someone subscribed to ChocolateDispensed")); dispenser.Mock.Setup.ChocolateDispensed.OnUnsubscribed .Do((target, method) => Console.WriteLine($"{method.Name} unsubscribed"));
To check that your code subscribed to an event, see Verify interactions: dispenser.Mock.Verify.ChocolateDispensed.Subscribed().Once();

Indexers are set up like properties, but take a value or a parameter matcher for each key. Without a setup, an indexer stores the values written to it per key, and returns the default value for keys that were never written. dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()] .InitializeWith(type => 20) .OnGet.Do((type, value) => Console.WriteLine($"Stock for {type} was read: {value}")); dispenser.Mock.Setup["Dark"] .InitializeWith(10) .OnSet.Do((type, value) => Console.WriteLine($"Stock for {type} was set to {value}"));

Use InitializeWith to give the indexer a start value. It keeps behaving like a normal indexer, so the setter changes the value and the getter returns the last value set for that key. The value can also be computed from the key: dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].InitializeWith(42); dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].InitializeWith(type => type.Length);

Set up the getter with Returns and Throws. Multiple calls define a sequence that starts over after the last entry: dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()] .Returns(1) .Returns(2) .Throws(new Exception("Error")) .Returns(4); You can also compute the value from the key(s), or from the key(s) and the current value: dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()] .Returns(type => type.Length); dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()] .Returns((type, current) => current + 10); // Increment by 10 each read

Register callbacks on the getter with OnGet and on the setter with OnSet. They can be parameterless, receive the value, or receive the key(s) followed by the value. Chain them on the same setup, because a second setup with the same matchers would replace the first one: dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()] .OnGet.Do((type, value) => Console.WriteLine($"Read this[{type}]: {value}")) .OnSet.Do((type, newValue) => Console.WriteLine($"Set this[{type}] to {newValue}")); Multiple callbacks form a sequence, like Returns and Throws: dispenser.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()] .OnGet.Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, … read")) .OnGet.Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … read")); When several setups match the same key, the one defined last wins.
Use .SkippingBaseClass() to prevent calls to the base class implementation for a single indexer, or MockBehavior.SkippingBaseClass() for the whole mock.

With C# 15, indexer keys accept predicates directly, in setups and verifications alike: dispenser.Mock.Setup[type => type.StartsWith("D")].Returns(10); dispenser.Mock.Verify[type => type.StartsWith("D")].Got().Once(); Only an indexer that is the sole indexer of its key count on the type takes union-typed keys; indexers sharing a key count keep the classic matcher/value overloads. See Union parameters for the details.

As for properties, the setup and verify members only offer the accessors that the mock actually intercepts: a get-only indexer has no OnSet, and a set-only indexer has neither OnGet, Returns, Throws nor InitializeWith. public interface IChocolateStorage { int this[string shelf] { get; } // no setter string this[int box] { set; } // no getter } IChocolateStorage storage = IChocolateStorage.CreateMock(); storage.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].Returns(3); storage.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<int>()].OnSet.Do(value => Console.WriteLine(value)); storage.Mock.Verify["top"].Got().Once(); storage.Mock.Verify[7].Set("Ada").Once(); // ❌ These do not compile: // storage.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<string>()].OnSet // storage.Mock.Setup[It.IsAny<int>()].Returns("Ada") // storage.Mock.Verify["top"].Set(3) // storage.Mock.Verify[7].Got() tip All callbacks and return values support conditional execution, repetition, parallel callbacks and access to the invocation counter. See Advanced callback features.

Use dispenser.Mock.Setup.MethodName(…) to set up a method. Pass a value or a parameter matcher for each parameter to decide which calls the setup applies to. With C# 15 you can also pass a predicate directly (see Union parameters).

Use .Returns(…) to specify the value to return. You can provide a value, a factory, or a factory that receives the method parameters. Use .Throws(…) to specify an exception to throw, either directly, as a factory or as a factory that receives the method parameters. // Return a fixed value dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Milk", It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true); // Compute the return value from the parameters dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns((type, amount) => amount <= 10); // Throw an exception dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Green", It.IsAny<int>()) .Throws<InvalidChocolateException>();

Call .Returns(…) and .Throws(…) multiple times to define a sequence. Each call uses the next entry; after the last entry the sequence starts again from the beginning: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .Throws(new Exception("Error")) .Returns(false); // Calls: true, throws, false, true, throws, false, … Mark the last entry with .Forever() to repeat it instead of starting over: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .Returns(true) .Returns(false).Forever(); // Calls: true, false, false, false, … See Advanced callback features to repeat entries (.For(n)), limit them (.Only(n)) or apply them conditionally (.When(…)).

For methods returning Task/Task<T> or ValueTask/ValueTask<T>, use .ReturnsAsync(…) and .ThrowsAsync(…) so that you don't have to wrap the value in a task yourself: public interface IChocolateDispenser { // the members from the core concepts, and: Task<int> DispenseAsync(string type, int amount); } dispenser.Mock.Setup.DispenseAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) .ReturnsAsync((_, amount) => amount) // First call returns the value of the `amount` parameter .ThrowsAsync(new TimeoutException()) // Second call returns a faulted task .ReturnsAsync(0).Forever(); // Subsequent calls return 0

Use .Do(…) to run code when the method is called. The callback can be parameterless or receive the method parameters: dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("White", It.IsAny<int>()) .Do((type, amount) => Console.WriteLine($"Dispensed {amount} {type} chocolate.")); .Do(…) can be combined with .Returns(…) and .Throws(…) on the same setup.

Class mocks call the base class implementation of a virtual method, and use its return value when the setup does not provide one. Use .SkippingBaseClass() on a setup to prevent this for a single method, or MockBehavior.SkippingBaseClass() for the whole mock. tip All callbacks and return values support conditional execution, repetition, parallel callbacks and access to the invocation counter. See Advanced callback features.
Without a setup, a property of a mock behaves like an auto-property: the getter returns the value that was last written, or the default value. Use dispenser.Mock.Setup.PropertyName to change this.

Use InitializeWith to give the property a start value. It keeps behaving like a normal property, so the setter changes the value and the getter returns the last value set: dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.InitializeWith(42); On a mock created with ThrowingWhenNotSetup(), every property access without a setup throws. Use Register() to allow access without providing a value: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); // Register the property without a value, so that accessing it does not throw dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed.Register();

Set up the getter with Returns and Throws. Multiple calls define a sequence that starts over after the last entry: dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .Returns(1) .Returns(2) .Throws(new Exception("Error")) .Returns(4); You can also compute the value from the current value: dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .Returns(current => current + 10); // Increment by 10 each read

Register callbacks on the getter with OnGet and on the setter with OnSet. They can be parameterless or receive the value. Chain them on the same setup, because a second dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed statement would replace the first one: dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .OnGet.Do(value => Console.WriteLine($"TotalDispensed was read: {value}")) .OnSet.Do(newValue => Console.WriteLine($"TotalDispensed changed to {newValue}")); Multiple callbacks form a sequence, like Returns and Throws: dispenser.Mock.Setup.TotalDispensed .OnGet.Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, … read")) .OnGet.Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Runs on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … read"));
Use .SkippingBaseClass() to prevent calls to the base class implementation for a single property, or MockBehavior.SkippingBaseClass() for the whole mock.

The setup and verify members only offer the accessors that the mock actually intercepts: a get-only property has no OnSet, and a set-only property has neither OnGet, Returns, Throws nor InitializeWith. Register() and SkippingBaseClass() are available on both. public interface IChocolateInventory { int RemainingBars { get; } // no setter string LastCountedBy { set; } // no getter } IChocolateInventory inventory = IChocolateInventory.CreateMock(); inventory.Mock.Setup.RemainingBars.Returns(3); inventory.Mock.Setup.LastCountedBy.OnSet.Do(value => Console.WriteLine(value)); inventory.Mock.Verify.RemainingBars.Got().Once(); inventory.Mock.Verify.LastCountedBy.Set("Ada").Once(); // ❌ These do not compile: // inventory.Mock.Setup.RemainingBars.OnSet // inventory.Mock.Setup.LastCountedBy.Returns("Ada") // inventory.Mock.Verify.RemainingBars.Set(3) // inventory.Mock.Verify.LastCountedBy.Got() The restriction also holds for the builders returned by Returns, Throws, Do and TransitionTo, so chaining never reaches an accessor that the mock does not intercept. Accessors that the mock cannot see The same applies when a property declares an accessor that your test assembly cannot see, such as { get; internal set; } on a type from an assembly that does not grant InternalsVisibleTo. Writes never reach the mock in that case, so only the getter is offered. See Mockolate0002 for when such a type is mockable at all. tip All callbacks and return values support conditional execution, repetition, parallel callbacks and access to the invocation counter. See Advanced callback features.

Some types need more than the generic setup and verification members. Mockolate supports them out of the box: Type What you get HttpClient Set up and verify HTTP calls by verb, URI, content and headers, and mock IHttpClientFactory. Delegates Mock Action, Func<T> and custom delegates; Mock.Setup(…) and Mock.Verify(…) take the delegate parameters directly. // HttpClient HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.CreateMock(); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org/api/chocolate*")) .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, "{\"type\":\"Dark\"}", "application/json"); // Delegates Func<int> nextAmount = Func<int>.CreateMock(); nextAmount.Mock.Setup().Returns(3);

Mockolate supports mocking delegates, including Action, Func<T> and custom delegates. Because a delegate has a single method, Mock.Setup(…) and Mock.Verify(…) are methods that take the delegate parameters directly.

// Mock an Action delegate Action myAction = Action.CreateMock(); myAction.Mock.Setup().Do(() => Console.WriteLine("Action invoked!")); // Mock a Func<T> delegate Func<int> myFunc = Func<int>.CreateMock(); myFunc.Mock.Setup().Returns(42); For custom delegates with parameters, pass a value or a parameter matcher for each parameter, including ref and out parameters: public delegate int Calculate(int x, string operation); public delegate void ProcessData(int input, ref int value, out int result); Calculate calculator = Calculate.CreateMock(); calculator.Mock.Setup(It.IsAny<int>(), "add") .Returns((x, operation) => x + 10); ProcessData processor = ProcessData.CreateMock(); processor.Mock.Setup(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsRef<int>(v => v + 1), It.IsOut(() => 100)); The setup supports the same options as a method setup: .Returns(…), .Throws(…), .Do(…), sequences and the advanced callback features.

// The Action was invoked at least once myAction.Invoke(); myAction.Mock.Verify().AtLeastOnce(); // The Func<T> was invoked exactly once _ = myFunc(); myFunc.Mock.Verify().Once(); // The custom delegate was invoked with "add" _ = calculator(5, "add"); calculator.Mock.Verify(It.IsAny<int>(), "add").Once(); // Use It.IsRef<T>() and It.IsOut<T>() to match any ref or out parameter int value = 0; processor(1, ref value, out int result); processor.Mock.Verify(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsRef<int>(), It.IsOut<int>()).Once();

Mockolate supports mocking HttpClient out of the box, with no special configuration required. You can set up, use, and verify HTTP interactions just like with any other class. The HTTP-specific matchers and ReturnsAsync overloads live in the Mockolate.Web namespace. using Mockolate.Web; HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.CreateMock(); httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); HttpResponseMessage result = await httpClient.PostAsync("https://testably.org/api/chocolate/dispense", new StringContent(""" { "type": "Dark", "amount": 3 } """, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")); await That(result.IsSuccessStatusCode).IsTrue(); httpClient.Mock.Verify.PostAsync( It.IsUri("*testably.org/api/chocolate/dispense*").ForHttps(), It.IsHttpContent("application/json").WithStringMatching("*\"type\": \"Dark\"*\"amount\": 3*")).Once(); note Under the hood, all setups, requests and verifications are forwarded to the SendAsync method of a mocked HttpMessageHandler. You can therefore mix string and Uri parameters between setup and verification, and a setup for GetAsync(string) also applies to calls of GetAsync(Uri).

Mockolate supports all standard HTTP methods: // GET httpClient.Mock.Setup .GetAsync(It.IsAny<string>()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)); // POST httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<HttpContent>()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); // PUT httpClient.Mock.Setup .PutAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<HttpContent>()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); // DELETE httpClient.Mock.Setup .DeleteAsync(It.IsAny<string>()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)); // PATCH httpClient.Mock.Setup .PatchAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<HttpContent>()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); .NET 8 or later for PatchAsync The PatchAsync setup and verification are available on .NET 8 or later. For all HTTP methods you can add an optional cancellation token parameter. If no parameter is provided, it matches any CancellationToken: CancellationTokenSource cts = new CancellationTokenSource(); httpClient.Mock.Setup .GetAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.Is(cts.Token)) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); await httpClient.GetAsync("https://example.com", cts.Token);
Use It.IsUri(string?) to match URIs using a wildcard pattern against the string representation of the URI. The pattern supports * to match zero or more characters and ? to match a single character.

Filter requests by URI scheme using .ForHttps() or .ForHttp(): // Match only HTTPS requests httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org*").ForHttps()) .Once(); // Match only HTTP requests httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org*").ForHttp()) .Never();
Filter requests by host using .WithHost(string). You can provide a wildcard pattern to match against the host name: httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithHost("*testably.org*")) .Once();
Filter requests on a specific port using .WithPort(int): httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithPort(443)) .Once();
Filter requests by path using .WithPath(string). You can provide a wildcard pattern to match against the path: httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithPath("/foo/*")) .Once();

Filter requests by query parameters using .WithQuery(...). You can provide one or many key-value pairs or a raw query string to match against the query parameters. The order of the key-value pairs does not matter: // Match query string containing "x=42" httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithQuery("x", "42")) .Once(); // Match query string containing "x=42" and "y=foo" (in any order) httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithQuery(("x", "42"), ("y", "foo"))) .Once(); // Match query string containing "x=42" and "y=foo" (in any order) httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithQuery("x=42&y=foo")) .Once();

Use It.IsHttpContent(string?) to match the HTTP content, optionally providing an expected media type header value: httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/json")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK));

To verify against the string content, use the following methods: .WithString(Func<string, bool>): to match the string content against the given predicate .WithString(string): to match the content exactly as provided .WithStringMatching(string): to match the content using wildcard patterns .WithStringMatching(string).AsRegex(): to match the content using regular expressions httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/json").WithStringMatching("*\"type\": \"Dark\"*")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); Add the .IgnoringCase() modifier to make the string matching case-insensitive.

To verify against the binary content, use the following methods: .WithBytes(Func<byte[], bool>): to match the binary content against the given predicate .WithBytes(byte[]): to match the content exactly as provided httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/octet-stream").WithBytes([0x01, 0x02, 0x03, ])) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK));

To verify against the URL-encoded form data content, use the following methods: .WithFormData(string, string): checks that the form-data content contains the provided key-value pair .WithFormData(IEnumerable<(string, string)>): checks that the form-data content contains the provided key-value pairs .WithFormData(string): checks that the form-data content contains the provided raw form data string httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/x-www-form-urlencoded").WithFormData("my-key", "my-value")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); As with query parameters, the order of the form-data key-value pairs does not matter. Add the .Exactly() modifier to also check that no other form data is present.

To verify against the HTTP content headers, use the following methods: .WithHeaders(string, HttpHeaderValue): checks that the content headers contain the provided key-value pair .WithHeaders(IEnumerable<(string, HttpHeaderValue)>): checks that the content headers contain all key-value pairs .WithHeaders(string): checks that the content headers contain the provided raw headers httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent().WithHeaders(("Content-Type", "application/json"), ("X-My-Header", "my-value"))) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent().WithHeaders(""" Content-Type: application/json X-My-Header: my-value """)) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); By default, only the content headers are checked, not the headers of the HttpRequestMessage. To check both, add the .IncludingRequestHeaders() modifier.

Overloads of .ReturnsAsync simplify specifying the return value for HTTP method setups. httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and no content .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a string content "some string content" .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, "some string content"); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a JSON content {"foo":"bar"} .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, "{\"foo\":\"bar\"}", "application/json"); byte[] bytes = new byte[] { /* ... */ }; httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a binary content with the provided bytes .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, bytes); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a PNG image content with the provided bytes .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, bytes, "image/png");

Use It.IsHttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod?) together with Setup.SendAsync(...) to match against the entire HttpRequestMessage, optionally restricted to a specific HTTP method. This is the catch-all entry point that the verb-specific overloads (GetAsync, PostAsync, …) route through internally; reach for it when you need the full request (e.g. to inspect headers, or to handle non-standard verbs like HEAD or OPTIONS). Chain builders to add constraints: .WhoseUriIs(string) / .WhoseUriIs(Action<IUriParameter>): same surface as It.IsUri(...). .WhoseContentIs(Action<IHttpContentParameter>) / .WhoseContentIs(string mediaType, …): same surface as It.IsHttpContent(...). .WithHeaders(...): require specific request headers. // Match any POST to /api/chocolate/dispense with a JSON body containing "Dark" httpClient.Mock.Setup .SendAsync(It.IsHttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post) .WhoseUriIs(uri => uri.WithPath("/api/chocolate/dispense")) .WhoseContentIs("application/json", c => c.WithStringMatching("*\"type\": \"Dark\"*"))) .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK);

When the code under test pulls clients from IHttpClientFactory and wraps them in using blocks (using HttpClient client = _factory.CreateClient("chocolate-api");), two naive mocking patterns both break: Returning the same mocked HttpClient instance from every CreateClient call throws ObjectDisposedException on the second call, because the first using block already disposed it. Returning a freshly created mocked HttpClient from a Returns(() => ...) factory avoids the disposal exception but spreads invocation history across many short-lived mocks, so verifications can no longer see the full call sequence. The fix is to mock the underlying HttpMessageHandler once and hand out fresh HttpClient wrappers that all share it. Because Mockolate intercepts on the handler, the registry (and therefore the invocation history) lives on the handler and survives any number of wrapper disposals. Pass disposeHandler: false when constructing each wrapper so that disposing the wrapper does not also dispose the shared handler. // One mocked handler shared by every HttpClient the factory hands out. HttpMessageHandler handler = HttpMessageHandler.CreateMock(); // Setup goes on any HttpClient wrapping the handler; the shared registry routes the // configuration to every wrapper that uses the same handler. HttpClient setupClient = HttpClient.CreateMock(handler, disposeHandler: false); setupClient.Mock.Setup .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org/api/chocolate/inventory/*").ForHttps()) .ReturnsAsync(() => new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); // The factory returns a fresh HttpClient each call, all sharing the handler. // `disposeHandler: false` keeps the shared handler alive when consumers `using` the client. IHttpClientFactory factory = IHttpClientFactory.CreateMock(); factory.Mock.Setup.CreateClient(It.IsAny<string>()) .Returns(() => HttpClient.CreateMock(handler, disposeHandler: false)); // The code under test can now safely use `using` blocks. Each call goes through the same // handler, so the invocation history is preserved across every disposed wrapper. foreach (string type in new[] { "Dark", "Milk", "White" }) { using HttpClient client = factory.CreateClient("chocolate-api"); _ = await client.GetAsync($"https://testably.org/api/chocolate/inventory/{type}"); } setupClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org/api/chocolate/inventory/*").ForHttps()) .Exactly(3); warning disposeHandler: false is the critical bit. HttpClient.Dispose() disposes its handler by default, which would tear down the shared mock after the first using block. Setup and verification can target any HttpClient wrapping the same handler. The setupClient above is just one convenient handle; the clients handed out by the factory work equally well.
Each section starts with a symptom and gives a short answer with a link to the detailed page. The limitations at the end list what Mockolate cannot mock and why.

CreateMock() and the Mock property are C# 14 extension members that the source generator emits into the Mockolate namespace. When the compiler does not find them, check: The using directive: add using Mockolate; (or a global using) to the test file. The SDK and the language version: the generator needs the compiler of the .NET 10 SDK. If your test project pins <LangVersion>, it must be 14 or later (or latest). An older compiler cannot load the generator, so it emits no mocks. The package reference: the generator and the analyzers are in the analyzers folder of the Mockolate package. A PackageReference that excludes the analyzers asset (with ExcludeAssets, or an IncludeAssets without it) also excludes the generator. The project language: the generator is packaged for C# projects only. If the IDE keeps showing outdated generated members after you fixed the cause, run dotnet clean and build again.
documents.s: CreateMock() or the Mock property does not exist

documents.t: Besides the mocks, the generator emits a fallback CreateMock() that accepts any type. The compiler picks it when the generator emitted no mock for your type, usually because the type cannot be mocked. Assigning its result to your type does not compile, and calling it throws a MockException: public class LockedChocolateDispenser { private LockedChocolateDispenser() { } } _ = LockedChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); Failure message This method should not be called directly. Either 'MyNamespace.LockedChocolateDispenser' is not mockable or the source generator did not run correctly. Check the type against the limitations. For most of them, the Mockolate0002 analyzer already fails the build with the reason: public sealed class SealedChocolateDispenser { } // Mockolate0002: Type 'MyNamespace.SealedChocolateDispenser' cannot be mocked: type is sealed SealedChocolateDispenser dispenser = SealedChocolateDispenser.CreateMock();

When the mocked type already has a member named Mock, the generator names the accessor Mockolate_Mock instead, so that your member stays reachable. If that name is taken as well, it appends a number (Mockolate_Mock__1, Mockolate_Mock__2, …). public interface IChocolateMachine { int Mock { get; } } IChocolateMachine machine = IChocolateMachine.CreateMock(); machine.Mockolate_Mock.Setup.Mock.Returns(4); await That(machine.Mock).IsEqualTo(4);
documents.s: The mock has Mockolate_Mock instead of Mock

documents.t: .Implementing<T>() returns a new mock and leaves the original one unchanged. Keep the returned reference, and reach the setups of the additional interface with Mock.As<T>(). See Implementing additional interfaces.
documents.s: .Implementing<T>() has no effect on my mock

documents.t: By default, a mock never fails for a missing setup. Methods return a default value (false, 0, an empty string, an empty collection, a completed task, or null for other reference types), and properties and indexers store the values written to them. A method that returns an interface or a class therefore returns null until you set it up. To fail on every call without a matching setup, create the mock with ThrowingWhenNotSetup(). To change the default value of a type, use WithDefaultValueFor<T>(…).
documents.s: A member without setup returns a value instead of failing

documents.t: A mock created with ThrowingWhenNotSetup() throws a MockNotSetupException for every call that no setup matches, also when other setups of the same member exist: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Dispense("Milk", 1); Failure message The method 'global::MyNamespace.IChocolateDispenser.Dispense(string, int)' was invoked without prior setup. For a property, the message reads The property '…' was accessed without prior setup. Add a setup for the reported member, or use a matcher such as It.IsAny<string>() so that the existing setup covers the call.

When several setups match a call, the one defined last wins. A general setup defined after a specific one therefore hides it. Every dispenser.Mock.Setup.X statement also starts a new setup, so chain everything that belongs to one setup. See What happens when the mock is called.

A class mock can only override virtual and abstract members. Other members always run the real implementation (see members that are not mocked). A virtual member also calls the base class implementation when a setup matches; the setup's return value takes precedence. Use SkippingBaseClass() to turn the base class calls off.
documents.s: My class mock runs the real implementation

documents.t: The count methods are extension methods in the Mockolate.Verify namespace. Add using Mockolate.Verify; to the test file. See Verify interactions.
documents.s: .Once() and the other count methods do not exist

documents.t: A verification without a count method checks nothing. Add a count such as .Once() or .AtLeastOnce(); the code fix adds .AtLeastOnce() for you. See Mockolate0001.

The MockVerificationException states the expected call with its arguments and how often it actually happened: dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); dispenser.Dispense("Milk", 2); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).AtLeast(3); Failure message Expected that mock invoked method Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) at least 3 times, but it did twice. When the count is lower than you expect, check: The arguments: a plain value matches with EqualityComparer<T>.Default, so a class without its own Equals only matches the same instance. Use It.Satisfies<T>(…) or a custom equality comparer instead. Background threads: if the code under test calls the mock asynchronously, the call may not have happened yet. Use Within(…). A monitor or a reset: interactions outside a monitor scope, or before ClearAllInteractions(), are not counted. A mock created with SkippingInteractionRecording() records nothing, so every verification on it throws a MockException.
documents.s: A verification fails although the method was called

documents.t: Mockolate generates mocks at compile time, so it can only override what C# lets a derived class override, and only what your test assembly can access. The generator skips what it cannot mock; the analyzers report most of these cases.

Type Reported by A struct, an enum, a record or a sealed class (delegates are supported) Mockolate0002 A type declared in the global namespace Mockolate0002 Any other kind of type, such as an array Mockolate0002 A type with an abstract member that your assembly cannot access, or whose signature uses a type your assembly cannot access Mockolate0002 A class in .Implementing<T>(): additional types must be interfaces Mockolate0002 A class without a public, protected or protected internal constructor whose parameter types your assembly can access no diagnostic; the fallback CreateMock() throws a MockException A nested type declared private or private protected no diagnostic; the fallback CreateMock() throws a MockException

These members keep their real behavior, or throw, and get no Setup or Verify members: Non-virtual members of a class cannot be overridden and always run the real implementation. If the class implements them for an interface, .Implementing<T>() makes the calls through the interface mockable. Sealed members (sealed override) cannot be overridden either. Static members of a class cannot be virtual. static abstract and static virtual interface members are supported on .NET 8 or later; see Static interface members. internal and private protected virtual members declared in another assembly are only overridden when that assembly grants your test assembly InternalsVisibleTo. Virtual members whose signature uses an inaccessible type: when the return type, a parameter type or a generic constraint names a type your test assembly cannot access (including a protected nested type), the member is not overridden, because the setup and verification members would have to name that type. Members with ref structs other than Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> in an unsupported position, such as a returned ref struct, have no setup; calling them throws a NotSupportedException, unless a virtual class member can forward to the base class. The Mockolate0003 warning lists the cases and the requirements for ref struct parameters. Generic methods with an allows ref struct type parameter that is used in the return type or in a parameter type throw a NotSupportedException when called. No analyzer reports them. For the abstract counterparts of the inaccessible members above, the mock cannot be created at all, and Mockolate0002 reports the type. Members with more than four parameters For members with more than four parameters, a setup or verification takes either values for all parameters or matchers for all of them. See Mixing values and matchers.

Every interaction with a mock is recorded. Use dispenser.Mock.Verify to check that methods, properties, indexers or events were used with specific arguments, and how many times: dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5).AtLeastOnce(); A verification fails with a MockVerificationException that describes the expected and the actual calls. Arguments are matched with the same values and matchers as in setups. note The count methods are extension methods in the Mockolate.Verify namespace, so add using Mockolate.Verify; to your test files.

Method The interaction occurred … .Never() never .Once() exactly once .Twice() exactly twice .Exactly(n) exactly n times .AtLeastOnce() at least once .AtLeastTwice() at least twice .AtLeast(n) at least n times .AtMostOnce() at most once .AtMostTwice() at most twice .AtMost(n) at most n times .Between(min, max) between min and max times (inclusive) .Times(predicate) a number of times that satisfies the predicate

// Dispense("Dark", 5) was called at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5).AtLeastOnce(); // Dispense was never called with "White" and any amount dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("White", It.IsAny<int>()).Never(); // Dispense was called exactly twice, with any arguments dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(Match.AnyParameters()).Exactly(2); // Dispense was called an even number of times dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Times(count => count % 2 == 0); You can also verify how often a specific setup was used: IMethodSetup setup = dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", 5).Returns(true); // Act dispenser.Mock.VerifySetup(setup).AtLeastOnce();

// The property 'TotalDispensed' was read at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Got().AtLeastOnce(); // The property 'TotalDispensed' was set to 42 exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Set(42).Once(); // The property 'TotalDispensed' was set to a value greater than 10 dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Set(It.Satisfies<int>(v => v > 10)).AtLeastOnce();

// The indexer was read with the key "Dark" exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify["Dark"].Got().Once(); // The indexer was set for the key "Milk" to 7 at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify["Milk"].Set(7).AtLeastOnce(); Both the keys and the value accept matchers.

// A handler was subscribed to 'ChocolateDispensed' at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify.ChocolateDispensed.Subscribed().AtLeastOnce(); // A handler was unsubscribed from 'ChocolateDispensed' exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify.ChocolateDispensed.Unsubscribed().Once();

Use Then to verify that calls occurred in a specific order: dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1).Then( m => m.Dispense("Milk", 2), m => m.Dispense("White", 3)); If the order is different or a call is missing, a MockVerificationException is thrown.

If the code under test calls the mock from a background thread, use Within(TimeSpan) to wait until the expected interactions occurred: // Wait up to 1 second for Dispense("Dark", 5) to be called dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5) .Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)) .AtLeastOnce(); Use WithCancellation(CancellationToken) to wait until the token is canceled instead. If you combine it with Within, both the timeout and the token are respected. Both block the test until the expected interactions occurred, or throw a MockVerificationException when the time is up. tip aweXpect.Mockolate offers awaitable verifications, including an asynchronous Within(TimeSpan) that does not block the test thread: await That(dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5)).AtLeastOnce().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
Monitor interactions to only count the interactions within a scope. Check for unexpected interactions to check that all interactions were verified or all setups were used.
